lesson.title: Visiting Every Element: List Traversal
lesson.summary: Traversal means visiting every element of a list in order, one at a time, which is the foundation for searching, summing, printing, and transforming data.
lesson.body:
Almost everything useful you do with a list, adding up its numbers, searching for a name, printing a report, requires looking at each element in turn. That process, walking through a list from the first element to the last, is called traversal. You have already met the two tools that make traversal possible: the for loop, which repeats a block of code, and the list itself, which holds the sequence of values to repeat over.

The most direct way to traverse a list in Python is to let the for loop hand you each value directly, without you managing an index yourself:

```python
prices = [12, 45, 7, 23]
total = 0
for price in prices:
    total = total + price
print(total)
```

This prints:

```
87
```

Each pass through the loop, price takes on the next value from prices in order: 12, then 45, then 7, then 23. total accumulates the running sum, and by the time the loop finishes visiting every element, it holds 12 + 45 + 7 + 23, which is 87. This is traversal in its cleanest form: visit each item once, do something with it, move on.

There is also an index based way to traverse a list, using a while loop and a counter that tracks position rather than value:

```python
prices = [12, 45, 7, 23]
i = 0
while i < len(prices):
    print(prices[i])
    i = i + 1
```

This prints:

```
12
45
7
23
```

Both versions visit the same four values in the same order, the difference is only in mechanics. The while loop needs you to check the stopping condition, i < len(prices), and manually advance i each time, which means it is easy to make an off by one mistake if you forget to update i or use the wrong comparison. The for loop hands you the values directly and stops automatically once the list is exhausted, which is why Python programmers reach for it by default whenever they just need the values and not necessarily the positions. That for style traversal is common enough that it deserves its own closer look next.
